Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 38

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Negative Emotions: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Vignette:
# Carlos

Carlos was sixty-two when the truck hit him. He had been driving home from an evening rehearsal in his car, a 2008 sedan he had owned for eleven years, moving through the intersection on a green light when a delivery truck ran the red from his left. The impact came without warning—a crushing force that crumpled the driver's side door inward, the sound of metal screaming, the sensation of his body being thrown sideways as the airbag detonated. For a moment afterward, there was silence. Then pain. Then the smell of coolant and burnt rubber. He remembered the paramedics' voices, remembered being lifted onto a stretcher, remembered the hospital ceiling moving past him in fragments. The physical injuries—a fractured collarbone, three broken ribs, a concussion—had healed within months. It was now nearly two years later, and Carlos had come to understand that the damage the truck had done to his body was nothing compared to what it had done to his mind.

Before the collision, Carlos had been a professional dancer for forty years. He taught at a studio in the city and performed in local productions—contemporary work, mostly, though he had trained in classical ballet as a young man in Mexico. His body was his language. Movement was how he spoke to the world, how he understood himself. In the weeks after the accident, as his ribs began to knit back together, he had tried to return to the studio. But something had fractured that the doctors could not see. On his first day back, standing in front of the mirror in the rehearsal space, he had felt a sudden, overwhelming urge to leave his body entirely—to step outside of it, to blank it out, to make it not real. The sensation was so powerful that he had excused himself and sat alone in the office for an hour, breathing slowly, trying to find his way back into his own skin. He had come to believe that his body was no longer safe, that if he remained present in it, something terrible would happen again. So he had begun to deliberately dissociate during classes, to float above himself as he demonstrated combinations to his students, watching from somewhere outside his own flesh. It was the only way he could make himself move without panic.

The dissociation had become a habit. Every evening, when Carlos tried to sleep, the moment his head touched the pillow, images from the collision would surface—not clear memories, but fragmented sensations: the lurch of the impact, the sound of glass, a flash of the truck's grille. He could not put any of it into words. When he tried to describe what happened to his wife, María, he would open his mouth and find only silence, or fragments that made no sense. Instead of fighting the images, he had begun to stay awake. He would sit in the living room until two or three in the morning, watching television with the volume low, or reading novels, delaying the moment when sleep might come and bring the memories with it. María had noticed. She had stopped asking him to come to bed.

The shame that accompanied his memories was suffocating. When he did allow himself to recall the accident—usually against his will, when a car horn or the smell of exhaust triggered the moment back to him—he felt not just fear but a deep, corrosive sense of humiliation. He had come to believe that the accident had happened because of who he was, because something in his character had made him vulnerable, had made him unable to protect himself. A better man would have seen the truck coming. A stronger man would have reacted faster. The fact that the other driver had run a red light was irrelevant; Carlos was certain that he bore responsibility for what had occurred.

In the studio, he had begun to scan for exits the moment he entered a room. He positioned himself near doors during classes, and he found himself watching the windows obsessively, as if the truck might somehow come through them. Three weeks ago, a student had placed a hand on his shoulder during a correction, and Carlos had recoiled violently, his body flooding with alarm at the unexpected touch. The student had looked hurt. After that, Carlos had requested that staff and students ask permission before approaching him. His students had begun to keep their distance. Enrollment in his classes had dropped.

It was María who had finally insisted he seek help. She had found him one morning at four a.m., still awake, still trying not to think about the crash, still trying not to feel. She had taken his hand—carefully, so as not to startle him—and told him that she could not watch him disappear any longer. She had made the appointment herself. Now, sitting in the therapist's office, Carlos felt a thin thread of hope alongside his fear. He was terrified that he would never dance again, never feel joy or presence in his own body. But he was also, for the first time in two years, ready to try.
